misconceptions.baseline-first: A score like 80% sounds good on its own; learners do not ask what a model that ignores the input would get.
misconceptions.test-score-error-bars: Learners read 84% vs 82% on a small test set as a real difference.
misconceptions.learning-curves: More data always improves a model; it does nothing for a model too simple to fit.
misconceptions.missing-data-signal: A blank is neutral, so filling it with the mean is harmless.
misconceptions.temporal-split: Shuffling rows before splitting is always fair; with time series it lets the model see tomorrow.
misconceptions.group-split-leakage: Rows are independent, so a random row split is honest even when one person contributes many rows.
misconceptions.resampling-miscalibrates: Oversampling the rare class fixes imbalance for free; the model now over-predicts it.
misconceptions.online-learning-stream: A model must see all its data at once; one-pass updates can track a stream and drift with it.
misconceptions.logistic-regression: A classifier outputs yes or no; a linear model can output a calibrated probability that bends near the boundary.
misconceptions.polynomial-features: Linear models only fit straight lines; linear means linear in the weights, not the input.
misconceptions.outlier-leverage: One point among fifty cannot move a fit much; a point far along x has outsized leverage.
misconceptions.lasso-sparsity: All penalties shrink weights the same way; the corner of the L1 diamond zeros them.
misconceptions.correlated-coefficients: A coefficient measures how much a feature matters; with correlated features it is not even stable.
misconceptions.knn-choosing-k: More neighbours always means a better vote.
misconceptions.svm-widest-margin: Any separating line is as good as another, and every point shapes it.
misconceptions.kernel-trick: If no line separates the classes, a linear method is hopeless.
misconceptions.soft-margin: A good classifier must get every training point right.
misconceptions.naive-bayes-double-counting: Two clues that always appear together should count as two pieces of evidence.
misconceptions.deep-tree-memorises: A tree that is 100% right on training data has learned the rule.
misconceptions.random-forest-decorrelation: Averaging many copies of the best tree helps; identical trees make identical mistakes.
misconceptions.k-means-forced-k: Clusters the algorithm returns are clusters that exist.
misconceptions.k-means-initialisation: k-means has one answer for a dataset; it finds a local optimum that depends on the start.
misconceptions.dbscan-density: Clusters are round blobs around a centre.
misconceptions.hierarchical-cut: The data decides how many groups there are; here the analyst chooses by where to cut.
misconceptions.pca-compression: Dropping dimensions always throws away most of the information.
misconceptions.tsne-distances-mislead: Distances and cluster sizes in a 2-D embedding plot reflect the real data.
misconceptions.random-projection: Projecting onto random directions scrambles structure; for distances it barely does.
misconceptions.feature-hashing: Collisions between features must ruin a model; a few rare collisions cost little accuracy.
misconceptions.softmax-scores: Softmax shares probability in proportion to the scores; it exaggerates gaps exponentially.
misconceptions.universal-approximation: Fitting a complicated shape needs a complicated, hand-designed model.
misconceptions.recurrent-memory-fades: A network that reads word by word remembers the whole sentence equally.
misconceptions.gnn-message-passing: Neural nets only take grids or sequences; a graph net passes messages along edges, k hops in k layers.
misconceptions.weight-init-scale: Starting weights do not matter because training fixes them.
misconceptions.exploding-gradients: A loss spike means the data was bad; often it is one oversized gradient step.
misconceptions.lr-schedule-warmup: There is one right learning rate for the whole run.
misconceptions.adam-per-weight-steps: One global step size suits weights whose gradients differ a hundredfold.
misconceptions.dead-relu: Every unit keeps learning as long as training runs.
misconceptions.double-descent: Test error rises forever with model size once a model can fit the training set (the U-curve).
misconceptions.grokking: Once training accuracy is perfect nothing more is being learned. Toy must reproduce it (modular arithmetic) in the browser; build risk.
misconceptions.pruning-most-weights: Every weight in a trained network is needed.
misconceptions.convolution-learned-filters: People program the features a vision model looks for. Differs from cs:edge-filter (hand-made differencing) because here the filter values are trained.
misconceptions.receptive-field-growth: A 3x3 filter can only ever see 3x3 pixels, so a CNN cannot see whole objects.
misconceptions.pooling-stride: Downsampling throws information away evenly; max-pooling keeps whether a feature was there, not exactly where.
misconceptions.translation-equivariance: A network must learn a cat separately at every position in the frame.
misconceptions.cnn-not-rotation-invariant: A CNN recognises shapes in any orientation the way people do.
misconceptions.feature-hierarchy: Each layer of a vision model does the same job; later layers combine earlier detectors into larger patterns.
misconceptions.cnn-data-efficiency: A more flexible network is always better; the dense net can fit anything, so it needs far more examples.
misconceptions.residual-connections: Adding layers can only help; without a skip path, a deeper plain net trains worse than a shallow one.
misconceptions.data-augmentation: Every transformation is label-preserving; a flipped 6 can become a 9.
misconceptions.transfer-learning: A new task needs a model trained from scratch on lots of new data.
misconceptions.texture-bias: Vision models recognise objects by their outline as people do. Real-system claim: cite the study and reproduce in the toy.
misconceptions.how-llms-are-trained: Chatbots are programmed with answers or look them up in a database.
misconceptions.knowledge-cutoff: A chatbot knows today's news unless a tool fetches it.
misconceptions.pretraining-data-mix: Model abilities come from the architecture, not from what text went in.
misconceptions.training-data-dedup: Every training document is seen once and weighs the same; a text copied 1,000 times is far likelier to be recited.
misconceptions.compute-optimal-scaling: Bigger models are always better for the same compute.
misconceptions.instruction-tuning: Fine-tuning reliably teaches a model new facts.
misconceptions.rlhf-kl-leash: More optimisation against the learned reward always makes the model better.
misconceptions.dpo-direct-preference: Learning from preferences requires a reward model and an RL loop.
misconceptions.ai-feedback-rlaif: Replacing human raters with a model removes rater bias.
misconceptions.lora-low-rank: Fine-tuning must rewrite all the weights, so it needs a data centre.
misconceptions.quantization-bits: Cutting precision by 4x cuts quality by 4x.
misconceptions.distillation-soft-labels: A small model trained on a big model's outputs only copies its final answers.
misconceptions.kv-cache: Each new token re-reads the whole prompt from scratch.
misconceptions.mixture-of-experts: A model with 8x the parameters costs 8x as much per token.
misconceptions.speculative-decoding: Faster generation must mean lower-quality text; here the output is the same.
misconceptions.rope-rotary-positions: Position is a number stamped on each word; rotation makes attention depend on relative offset.
misconceptions.multi-head-attention: One attention pattern can capture who-did-what and which-word-is-next at once.
misconceptions.causal-mask: A model trained on whole sentences could cheat by reading ahead; the mask removes the answer.
misconceptions.in-context-learning: The model learns permanently from a conversation.
misconceptions.chain-of-thought: A model either knows the answer or not; generating intermediate tokens adds sequential steps it can use.
misconceptions.test-time-compute-voting: A model's accuracy on a question is fixed; spending more samples changes it.
misconceptions.beam-search: Keeping more candidates always gives better text (it can favour short, bland output).
misconceptions.lost-in-the-middle: Anything inside the context window is used equally. Real-system claim: cite and mark as about real models.
misconceptions.contrastive-embeddings: Embeddings are designed by hand or learned from labels; here the pairs are the only signal.
misconceptions.hybrid-keyword-vector-search: Vector search beats keyword search everywhere; it misses rare exact strings like part numbers.
misconceptions.autoencoder-bottleneck: A network asked to copy its input learns nothing; the bottleneck forces a summary.
misconceptions.vae-smooth-latent: Any point between two codes in an autoencoder decodes to a blend; in a plain one it decodes to garbage.
misconceptions.gan-forger-detective: The generator copies real images; it never sees them, only the detective's verdict.
misconceptions.gan-mode-collapse: A generator that fools the detector has learned the whole data.
misconceptions.diffusion-denoising: Image generators collage or retrieve stored pictures.
misconceptions.diffusion-step-count: Generation is one jump from noise to picture.
misconceptions.classifier-free-guidance: Following the prompt harder is free; it trades away diversity.
misconceptions.latent-diffusion: Diffusion works pixel by pixel at full size.
misconceptions.normalising-flows: You cannot both sample and compute exact probabilities from a generative model.
misconceptions.generative-memorisation: Generators never reproduce training data; duplicates are the exception that gets memorised.
misconceptions.generative-eval-tradeoff: One quality score can rank generators; a model can be realistic and repetitive.
misconceptions.mdp-basics: An RL agent is told the right move, as with labelled data; it only gets a score, often late.
misconceptions.value-vs-reward: The best move is the one with the biggest immediate reward.
misconceptions.policy-from-values: Policy and value are two names for the same thing.
misconceptions.bellman-backup: To value a square you must simulate every future path from it; each square only needs its neighbours' values.
misconceptions.monte-carlo-vs-td: You must finish an episode to learn anything from it.
misconceptions.td-error-surprise: An expected reward teaches as much as an unexpected one.
misconceptions.q-learning: An agent needs a map of the world to choose good moves.
misconceptions.sarsa-vs-q-cliff: Every learner converges to the same path; off-policy learning ignores its own exploration slips.
misconceptions.q-overestimation: Taking the best estimate gives an unbiased estimate of the best.
misconceptions.deep-q-function-approx: An RL agent must visit every state to value it.
misconceptions.experience-replay: Learning in the order experiences happen is the most faithful way.
misconceptions.policy-gradient: Learning to act needs a value for every state.
misconceptions.policy-gradient-baseline: If every reward is positive, every action gets reinforced equally hard.
misconceptions.actor-critic: Value methods and policy methods are rival camps; actor-critic uses both.
misconceptions.ppo-clipping: A bigger update after a great run is always better.
misconceptions.ucb-optimism: Exploring means choosing at random; UCB explores where uncertainty is largest.
misconceptions.thompson-sampling: Randomness in choice is wasted effort; sampling beliefs explores in proportion to doubt.
misconceptions.sparse-reward-exploration: Given enough time random exploration finds any reward; the odds shrink exponentially with path length.
misconceptions.curiosity-noisy-tv: Rewarding novelty always makes an agent explore usefully.
misconceptions.credit-assignment: The last move before a reward gets the credit.
misconceptions.reward-shaping: Any helpful extra reward keeps the goal the same; only potential-based shaping is guaranteed to.
misconceptions.model-based-planning: RL always learns by trial and error in the real world.
misconceptions.model-error-compounding: A model 99% accurate per step is 99% accurate over a long plan.
misconceptions.mcts-playouts: Game AIs search every move to the end; MCTS samples and focuses.
misconceptions.self-play: An agent needs expert opponents or human games to get strong.
misconceptions.offline-rl-extrapolation: With enough logged data you can learn any policy without acting.
misconceptions.behaviour-cloning-drift: Copying demonstrations perfectly gives expert performance; small slips lead to states the expert never showed.
misconceptions.dagger-correction: More expert demonstrations fix cloning drift; it needs labels on the learner's own states.
misconceptions.inverse-rl-goal-inference: Demonstrations show what to do, and that is all they hold; they also carry evidence about what the demonstrator wants.
misconceptions.reward-ambiguity: Behaviour pins down a single true reward.
misconceptions.boltzmann-rational-demos: A demonstrator's mistakes are noise to throw away.
misconceptions.max-entropy-irl: Choose the reward that makes the expert look most decisive.
misconceptions.irl-reward-transfer: Imitation and inverse RL learn the same thing; only the goal transfers when the layout changes.
misconceptions.rlhf-as-irl: RLHF is people writing rules for the model.
misconceptions.agent-loop: An agent is a smarter model; it is the same model in a loop with tools.
misconceptions.tool-call-request: The model itself searches the web or runs the code.
misconceptions.agent-checkpoint-recovery: A 95%-reliable agent finishes 95% of 20-step tasks. Differs from books:checklist-steps-compound by showing what verification and retry recover.
misconceptions.plan-vs-react: A complete plan up front is always better than deciding step by step.
misconceptions.task-decomposition: Breaking a task up only adds overhead.
misconceptions.agent-memory-files: An assistant remembers past conversations the way a person does.
misconceptions.context-compaction-loss: A summary keeps everything important; what counts as important is decided before you know the future.
misconceptions.least-privilege-agents: Safety comes from the model behaving well; permissions bound the damage when it does not.
misconceptions.checker-shared-blind-spots: Two copies of the same model checking each other are as good as two independent checkers.
misconceptions.agent-cost-growth: A 40-step run costs twice a 20-step run.
misconceptions.benchmark-contamination: A high benchmark score means the skill; if the questions were in the training text it may mean recall.
misconceptions.benchmark-saturation: A 1-point gain near the ceiling is as meaningful as one in the middle.
misconceptions.eval-prompt-sensitivity: A benchmark score is a property of the model alone.
misconceptions.pass-at-k: Scores reported at different k are comparable.
misconceptions.llm-judge-bias: An AI grader is neutral because it is a machine.
misconceptions.capability-elicitation: If an evaluation did not find a capability, the model does not have it.
misconceptions.maximum-likelihood: Fitting a model and computing probabilities are different jobs; minimising cross-entropy is maximising likelihood.
misconceptions.prior-as-regulariser: A prior is a bias that ruins objectivity; it is the same as a penalty and fades with data.
misconceptions.bayesian-posterior-lines: A fitted model is equally sure everywhere.
misconceptions.gaussian-process-uncertainty: A smooth curve through the points says nothing about where it might be wrong.
misconceptions.aleatoric-vs-epistemic: All uncertainty shrinks with more data.
misconceptions.ensemble-uncertainty: A single model's confidence is enough to know when to trust it.
misconceptions.ood-overconfidence: High confidence means the input is familiar.
misconceptions.conformal-sets: Honest uncertainty needs a Bayesian model; a held-out calibration set is enough for coverage.
misconceptions.gaussian-mixture-em: Each point belongs to exactly one cluster.
misconceptions.hidden-markov: Each observation should be read on its own; the hidden state carries information across time.
misconceptions.mcmc-random-walk: To sample from a distribution you must be able to compute it everywhere; ratios of neighbours are enough.
misconceptions.vi-mode-seeking: The best-fitting simple shape covers the whole posterior.
misconceptions.saliency-maps: A highlighted region is what the model "looked at".
misconceptions.permutation-importance: Feature importance shows what matters; with correlated features each looks unimportant.
misconceptions.shapley-credit: Credit is each feature's effect when changed alone; interactions get split by averaging over orders.
misconceptions.counterfactual-explanations: An explanation must list everything the model used; the nearest flip is often more useful and can be gamed.
misconceptions.probing-classifiers: If a concept can be decoded from a layer, the model uses it.
misconceptions.polysemantic-neurons: Each neuron stands for one thing.
misconceptions.superposition: A layer with 2 neurons can store at most 2 features.
misconceptions.sparse-autoencoder-features: Features are hidden in a model beyond reach; a sparse dictionary can recover them.
misconceptions.steering-vectors: Changing a model's behaviour needs retraining.
misconceptions.activation-patching: Correlation between an activation and the output shows it causes the output.
misconceptions.induction-heads: In-context learning is mysterious; part of it is a simple copying circuit.
misconceptions.cot-faithfulness: A model's shown steps are a faithful account of how it reached the answer.
misconceptions.object-detection-iou: A detection is right or wrong; the overlap threshold chooses which.
misconceptions.non-max-suppression: A detector naturally outputs one box per object.
misconceptions.segmentation-per-pixel: Finding an object and outlining it are the same task.
misconceptions.face-search-false-matches: A 99.9%-accurate face matcher is almost always right about a match.
misconceptions.spectrogram-picture: Speech recognisers listen to the waveform as we hear it.
misconceptions.ctc-alignment: Training speech recognition needs every sound labelled with its moment.
misconceptions.collaborative-filtering: Recommenders understand the content they recommend.
misconceptions.matrix-factorisation-tastes: Each person's taste needs hundreds of numbers to describe.
misconceptions.cold-start: A good recommender works from day one for a new user or item.
misconceptions.ranking-top-heavy: Getting the order right anywhere in the list counts the same.
misconceptions.persistence-forecast: A sophisticated forecasting model always beats repeating the last value.
misconceptions.seasonality-decomposition: A December spike means the trend changed.
misconceptions.forecast-fan: A model good at tomorrow is about as good at next month.
misconceptions.isolation-forest: Finding anomalies needs a description of normal.
misconceptions.drift-monitoring: You will know a model degraded when accuracy drops; labels often come weeks late.
misconceptions.offline-online-gap: A model that scores better on logged data will do better live.
misconceptions.sim-to-real-gap: A more accurate simulator is the only fix; randomising the simulator makes the policy robust.
misconceptions.evolution-strategies: You need gradients (backpropagation) to optimise a model.
misconceptions.cma-es-shape: A search should sample evenly in every direction; CMA-ES learns the valley's shape from its own winners.
misconceptions.es-step-size-adaptation: A fixed step size is fine if chosen well.
misconceptions.genetic-crossover: Mixing two good solutions gives a better one.
misconceptions.premature-convergence: Keeping only the best is the fastest route to the optimum.
misconceptions.deceptive-objective: Always moving closer to the goal is the way to reach it.
misconceptions.novelty-search: Ignoring the objective cannot beat optimising it.
misconceptions.map-elites: Search should return a single best answer.
misconceptions.behaviour-descriptor-choice: Diversity is objective; it is defined by the axes the designer picks.
misconceptions.pareto-front: Combining two goals into one weighted score finds every good trade-off; a weighted sum misses dents in the front.
misconceptions.random-vs-grid-search: A grid covers the space more systematically, so it must be better.
misconceptions.bayesian-optimisation: When each trial is costly, try the best-looking point; the most promising uncertain point is often better.
misconceptions.simulated-annealing-tour: A good search never takes a step that makes things worse.
misconceptions.ant-colony-tours: The most-used route is the best route; evaporation stops early luck from locking in.
misconceptions.ann-recall-speed: Vector search returns the exact nearest matches.
misconceptions.hnsw-navigable-graph: Search must compare the query with every stored vector; HNSW checks a few hundred, and greedy hops can stop at a near miss.
misconceptions.ivf-probe-clusters: Probing one cluster is enough; the true neighbour often sits just over a border.
misconceptions.product-quantization: Compressing a vector to 8 bytes destroys its meaning.
misconceptions.kd-tree-high-dim: A spatial index that is fast on a map is fast on embeddings. Differs from cs:algo-kd-nearest-pruning (how pruning works) by showing it failing as dimensions grow.
misconceptions.submodular-coverage-gains: Each pick's value is fixed; with coverage it depends on what is already picked. Differs from economics:diminishing-returns (one input's curve) by being about sets.
misconceptions.submodular-greedy-guarantee: Greedy can be arbitrarily bad (cs:greedy-failure); for diminishing-returns objectives it carries a guarantee.
misconceptions.mmr-diverse-retrieval: The top five matches are the five most useful.
misconceptions.injection-lethal-trifecta: Prompt injection is a chatbot saying something rude; with tools it can send data out.
misconceptions.jailbreak-surface-refusal: Safety training teaches the model what is harmful; it may learn what harmful requests look like.
misconceptions.backdoor-trigger: A model that passes every test is clean; a trigger absent from tests stays hidden.
misconceptions.membership-inference: Releasing a model, not the data, keeps the data private.
misconceptions.differential-privacy-noise: Removing names makes a dataset private.
misconceptions.text-watermark-paraphrase: AI text can be invisibly and permanently marked.
misconceptions.ai-detector-false-positives: A detector that is 95% accurate means a flagged essay is 95% likely AI-written.
misconceptions.deepfake-detector-arms-race: Detection technology will eventually win against fakes.
misconceptions.single-source-influence: Each source contributes equally, so opting out has the same effect for everyone. Legal claims stay out; only the mechanism is taught.
misconceptions.energy-train-vs-serve: Training is where AI's energy goes; at scale, serving queries can match or exceed it. Real-system numbers must be cited and dated.
misconceptions.task-exposure: A job is either automatable or not; it is a bundle of tasks with different exposure.
misconceptions.risk-tier-regulation: AI law regulates models; risk-based rules like the EU AI Act mostly regulate uses. Claims cite the legal text.
misconceptions.compute-thresholds: A compute threshold tracks capability exactly; efficiency gains move capability below it.
misconceptions.red-teaming-search: Normal use reveals a model's failures; rare ones need a targeted search.
misconceptions.behaves-when-watched: Passing a safety evaluation shows a model is safe in deployment.
misconceptions.options-keep-open: An agent only seeks power if told to; in many random goals, keeping options open is optimal.
misconceptions.automation-bias: A human in the loop catches the machine's errors; vigilance drops as the machine gets better.
